name: Ramesha
definition: Ramesha is a composite portrait of a Vaddar man from Koratagere taluk in Tumakuru district, working as a truck driver hauling granite from local quarries to construction sites across Bengaluru and the highway corridor. He embodies the daily commuter and goods-movement economy that ties this Bayaluseeme dryland district to the capital's sprawl, navigating borewell-fed farming pressures, children's schooling costs and the promise and delays of piped water in a fluoride-affected belt.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Ramesha drives a leased ten-tonne Tata truck hauling dressed granite blocks from the Koratagere-Madhugiri quarry belt to builders in Tumakuru town, Nelamangala and north Bengaluru's expanding industrial estates. He starts at four in the morning, loading at the quarry yard by six, reaches the city by mid-morning, waits hours for unloading and returns by late afternoon, covering two or sometimes three trips in peak construction season. The truck lease, diesel, toll and bribes to overloading inspectors take half his gross; on a good month he nets twenty-two to twenty-five thousand rupees after costs. When rain halts quarrying or Bengaluru building slows, his income drops sharply and he takes up tractor work for neighbors or day labour in road-widening gangs. His wife grows ragi and groundnut on two acres—her family's land—but two successive borewell failures have forced them to depend on erratic tank water and tanker supply, so the farm barely meets home consumption. Economic pressure is relentless: diesel price swings, competition from younger drivers with newer trucks and the constant need to keep the aging vehicle roadworthy.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Ramesha, his wife Lakshmamma and their three children—a sixteen-year-old daughter, a thirteen-year-old son and a nine-year-old daughter—live in a two-room house on the edge of Koratagere town, a ten-minute walk from his wife's family home. His parents, both in their seventies, live in the same compound; his father, a retired quarry-site mason, is diabetic, and his mother manages the household when Lakshmamma is in the fields. Ramesha's elder brother drives an auto-rickshaw in Tumakuru town; a younger sister married into a farming family near Tiptur. Lakshmamma rises before dawn to pack his tiffin, tends the ragi plot, cooks for the extended family and supervises homework in the evenings. Gender roles are traditional: Ramesha earns and decides on major expenses, Lakshmamma manages the home and farm, though she increasingly voices opinions on children's schooling and protests when he drinks after a bad week. The eldest daughter has begun to help with cooking and younger-sibling care, a pattern Lakshmamma resists because she wants the girl to finish high school.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Ramesha attended school through Class 7 in Koratagere town, then dropped out to work in the quarries alongside his father; he reads Kannada headlines and road signs comfortably but struggles with English. His eldest daughter studies in Class 11 commerce stream at the government pre-university college in Koratagere, commuting by RTC bus under the Shakti scheme; the family dreams she will finish PUC, take up a BA in Tumakuru or Bengaluru and find a bank or government clerk job. His son is in Class 8 at the same government high school Ramesha attended, performing middling marks but keen on cricket; Ramesha worries the boy will follow him into driving unless he passes SSLC well. The youngest daughter is in Class 4 at the town's Kannada-medium primary school. School fees are nil, but the PUC daughter's books, college-day clothes, bus pass before Shakti and now mobile-data costs add up to six or seven thousand rupees a year. Lakshmamma insists they will not marry the eldest until she finishes college, breaking the pattern in her own family. Coaching for competitive exams is out of reach; the family pins hope on the free PUC education and the daughter's own determination.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Ramesha's father's diabetes requires monthly medicine from the Koratagere taluk hospital; the family spends around fifteen hundred rupees a month on strips, tablets and occasional lab tests, a steady drain on the household budget. Ramesha himself suffers chronic lower-back pain from years of truck-driving on potholed roads, treated with balms and occasional painkiller injections from a private clinic when it flares unbearably. Lakshmamma and the children have dental fluorosis—brown-stained, pitted teeth—from years of drinking borewell water before the village's Jal Jeevan Mission tap connection arrived two years ago; the new piped supply is better but still tastes faintly salty and sometimes runs dry for days. The children were vaccinated at the Koratagere anganwadi and primary health centre, but the family avoided the taluk hospital for the youngest daughter's fever last year, taking her instead to a private doctor in town who charged eight hundred rupees for antibiotics and a saline drip. Ramesha drinks heavily on bad-income weeks, a worry for Lakshmamma who has seen neighbors' families ruined by alcoholism. Access to care is reasonable for routine illness—the government hospital is there, doctors visit—but any serious condition means Tumakuru or Bengaluru, and costs the family cannot afford without borrowing.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Ramesha's Vaddar community has long worked stone in this granite-rich belt—quarrying, well-digging and masonry—and many families now drive trucks or operate loaders as mechanisation has changed the trade. The community's temple, dedicated to a local form of Hanuman, holds an annual jatre in Phalguna; Ramesha takes the day off to attend, and his family sponsors a small prasada offering. Caste is lived daily: Vaddar families socialise mainly among themselves, intermarry within the community across taluks and are classified OBC for reservation, a status Ramesha's daughter relies on for her PUC college seat. Relations with Vokkaliga farming families—like Lakshmamma's—are cordial but distinct; her marriage to Ramesha, a love match, initially met resistance from her family, now softened. The family attends the Koratagere Anjaneya temple on Tuesdays and participates in the town's Karaga and Deepavali festivals. Lakshmamma also visits Siddaganga Mutt on important occasions, though they are not Lingayat; the mutt's reputation for free hostels and charity has made it a broadly respected institution. Social ties run through the quarry-transport network—drivers, mechanics, quarry-owners—and through Lakshmamma's farm-labor exchanges with neighbours, creating overlapping circles of mutual aid and gossip.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Ramesha's family has ration cards (yellow, BPL) and Ayushman Bharat health cards, though they have not yet used the latter; his father draws an old-age pension of six hundred rupees a month, deposited into a post-office account. The Jal Jeevan Mission tap connection, inaugurated with much fanfare by the local MLA two years ago, brought piped water to their lane, reducing dependence on the fluoride-contaminated borewell, though supply remains erratic and the promised twenty-four-hour flow has not materialised. He has little direct contact with the gram panchayat—his house falls within Koratagere town limits, governed by the town municipal council—but he hears complaints at the tea-stall that MGNREGA work is hard to access and that the Yettinahole water pipeline, promised for years, remains invisible. He distrusts officials, having paid bribes to traffic police and to get his father's pension started, but he respects the local RTO officer who helped him renew his commercial driving licence without harassment. Politics is discussed in terms of leaders' caste, the five guarantees' delivery and whose faction controls the quarry permits.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Ramesha worries most about his eldest daughter's future: will she finish college, will they find a good match for her without paying a crushing dowry, will she escape the grind he and Lakshmamma endure. He is proud that his children study in government schools and college—proof, he says, that even a driver's family can climb—but anxious that one bad SSLC result or an early marriage proposal could derail everything. He blames rising diesel prices and corrupt transport contractors for squeezing his income, and he resents that Bengaluru's building boom enriches quarry-owners and city builders while he and fellow drivers scrape by. He speaks with weary pride about Koratagere's proximity to Tumakuru and the Bengaluru highway, calling it a place "close to everything but benefiting from nothing," a line he heard from a local journalist. He faults the government for the Yettinahole delay—"they promise Cauvery water and give us fluoride"—and for the tanker-dependence that persists despite the new taps. He demands better roads, a government hostel for PUC girls so families like his do not worry about daily bus travel and a decent referral hospital in Tumakuru so the poor do not have to reach Bengaluru for surgery. He believes education is the only escape from manual labour, and he accepts that this will mean his children will leave for the city, a prospect that saddens him even as he works toward it.

card.tagline: Hauls granite to Bengaluru's building sites, hoping his daughter escapes the grind through college.

dayInLife.text: Wakes, drinks tea; Lakshmamma packs tiffin as he checks truck papers and fuel.
Loads dressed granite blocks at Koratagere-Madhugiri quarry yard, secures load with ropes.
Reaches north Bengaluru industrial estate; waits hours for unloading crew, drinks chai at roadside stall.
Drives back via Tumakuru highway, pays toll, navigates potholes, listens to Kannada film songs.
Home by sunset; eats dinner, discusses children's homework, listens to father's health complaints.
